newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-SANDELIN PUTT SINKS MONTGOMERIE AND SCOTLAND.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-SANDELIN PUTT SINKS MONTGOMERIE AND SCOTLAND.

text.p: A 110-foot birdie putt by Jarmo Sandelin at the 16th helped sink world number two Colin Montgomerie as unseeded Sweden stunned holders Scotland 2-1 on the opening day of the Alfred Dunhill Cup.
Sandelin's victory by 68 to 69 in the decisive third match of the tie on Thursday left the Scots facing an uphill battle to retain their title.
They must win their remaining two group matches 3-0 and hope that Sweden lose one to reach Sunday morning's semifinals.
In the only other upset on the first day of round-robin group matches, England, unseeded for the first time in the 12 years of the event, beat eighth-seeded Spain 3-0.
Mark O'Meara, playing for the top-seeded U.S. team, flirted with the 10-under-par Old Course record of 62 set by compatriot Curtis Strange in 1987 but had to settle for a 63.

He made 10 birdies in the first 12 holes, including a record-tying eight in succession from the second for a course record-breaking outward nine of 28. But a double-bogey six at the tough 461-yard "Road Hole" 17th torpedoed his chance.
He collected his 11th birdie at the last.
O'Meara defeated Costantino Rocca, heroic loser of the 1995 British Open here, by seven shots as the Americans beat Italy 2-1 in group four, the group containing England.
Steve Stricker beat Silvio Grappasonni 68-75 but U.S. Tour money leader Phil Mickelson, winner of four titles this year, lost to Emanuele Canonica on the second playoff hole.
Fourth seeds Zimbabwe, last year's beaten finalists, had a battle on their hands before beating debutants India 2-1.
There were also 2-1 victories for second-seeded Australia over Japan, third seeds South Africa over Canada, sixth-seeded Ireland against Wales, and seventh seeds New Zealand over Germany.

Montgomerie, who on Sunday clinched his record-tying fourth successive European Order of Merit title, birdied the first three holes against Sandelin and the Swede admitted thinking: "Oh my God, this is going to be tough.
"But I've learned that if you find your own game and focus on making the putts you can recover," he said.
Two behind at the turn, he birdied the 11th and 12th and his huge putt at 16 clinched the victory as Montgomerie managed only pars on the last two holes.
Andrew Coltart, like Montgomerie a member of last year's winning team, had begun with a 67-70 win over Peter Hedblom but Patrick Sjoland levelled by beating Raymond Russell 68-69.
The Scots were unlucky to lose with a cumulative total of 11 under par. That was second only to the Americans' 13 under and one better than the Swedes.
"It would have beaten most teams," Montgomerie said ruefully.
The big Scot had good reason to feel aggrieved because Sandelin's approach to the 16th looked to be heading out of bounds.
"He even shouted 'fore' to warn the crowd. But the ball stayed in and he holed the putt to go one ahead.
"It looked as if I might be one or two ahead. Instead I parred the hole and lost it," said Montgomerie.
Zimbabwe, who Scotland will have to beat again when they clash on Saturday, struggled to subdue India, former world number one Nick Price beating Jeev Singh 70-71 in the deciding match.
Tony Johnstone went down 72-73 to Ali Sher but Mark McNulty beat Gauruv Ghei 70-73 after the Indian, like O'Meara, double-bogeyed the 17th.
"They had nothing to lose today and adopted the attitude that they could go for it. I was very impressed," Price said of the losing team.
Price's birdie at the 15th put him two ahead and he could afford his bogey five at the 17th.
